prompt: You write `var minutes: [Int] = []` inside a struct, with no access keyword. What level does it have?
hint: The table in section 02 marks one level as the default.

choices.text: `private`
choices.why: Private has to be written; it is the narrowest, not the default.

choices.text: `internal`
choices.why: Right: visible anywhere in the same module, and nowhere else.

choices.text: `public`, because the struct is visible
choices.why: Nothing becomes public without the word; that is section 03's whole first error.

choices.text: `fileprivate`, the file it was written in
choices.why: The file is narrower than the default, which is the whole module.

prompt: `Week.swift` holds a struct with `private var log` and, below it in the same file, a free function that reads `week.log`. Does it compile?
hint: Private covers a declaration and its extensions in the file.

choices.text: Yes, since `private` means the whole file
choices.why: That is `fileprivate`; `private` stops at the type and its extensions.

choices.text: Yes, as every function in a file is part of the type
choices.why: A free function belongs to no type.

choices.text: No: the function is outside the type and its extensions
choices.why: Right: that is why section 02 made `minutes` `fileprivate`, the level that covers a free function in the same file.

choices.text: No: `private` properties are readable only in `init`
choices.why: Every method of the type reads them, and extensions in the file do too.

prompt: A property is `internal` and used by twelve files of one module. You want to make it `private`. What is the cost?
hint: Section 02: widening is cheap, and the other direction is not.

choices.text: None; access levels change nothing at run time
choices.why: True about run time, and the twelve files stop compiling all the same.

choices.text: Each of those twelve uses must change first
choices.why: Right: narrowing breaks every use outside the new region, so you rewrite them through methods first.

choices.text: A warning in each file, and the program still builds
choices.why: Using an inaccessible name is an error, not a warning.

choices.text: The property has to become a `let`
choices.why: Access and mutability are separate questions.

prompt: `plan` imports `PlannerCore`, whose `struct Week` has no access keyword. What does the compiler say at `Week()` in `plan`?

choices.text: `'Week' is inaccessible due to 'internal' protection level`
choices.why: That message names something it can see; from `plan`, an internal type is not there at all.

choices.text: `cannot find 'Week' in scope`
choices.why: Right: outside its module an internal type does not exist.

choices.text: Nothing: the import makes every name visible
choices.why: An import brings in only what the other module marked public or wider.

choices.text: A warning that the type should be public
choices.why: It is an error, and the build fails.

prompt: `public struct Week` with public properties, and no `init` written. Why does `Week()` still fail in another module?
hint: Look at the note the compiler printed.

choices.text: Structs cannot be public
choices.why: The type was visible; only its initialiser was not.

choices.text: Another module has to call `Week.init()` in full
choices.why: `Week()` and `Week.init()` are the same call to the same internal initialiser.

choices.text: The library was not rebuilt after the change
choices.why: `swift build` rebuilds what changed; the message is about access, not about an old build.

choices.text: The generated initialiser is `internal`
choices.why: Right: the note shows `internal init()`. A public type needs a public `init` written by hand.

prompt: Section 03's package has a library and an executable. How many modules does it build?
A unit of code compiled together and imported by name, such as `Foundation` or `PlannerCore`, is a ___.
What does `public private(set) var minutes` allow another module to do?

choices.text: Read `minutes` whenever it likes, but never assign to it
choices.why: Right: the getter is public and the setter is private.

choices.text: Read and replace `minutes`, but not append to it
choices.why: Replacing needs the setter just as appending does.

choices.text: Nothing; `private` wins over `public`
choices.why: The two words cover the getter and the setter separately.

choices.text: Read and write it, with a warning
choices.why: Writing it from outside is an error.

prompt: `week.minutes.append(45)` in `plan` is refused, though only appending. Why?

choices.text: `append` is a private method of `Array`
choices.why: `append` is public in the standard library; the setter of `minutes` is what is missing.

choices.text: Changing the array needs the setter, and it is private
choices.why: Right: `cannot use mutating member on immutable value: 'minutes' setter is inaccessible`.

choices.text: `week` was declared with `let`
choices.why: It was a `var`; the message names the setter.

choices.text: Arrays from another module are copied and cannot change
choices.why: A module boundary does not make a value immutable; the access level of the setter does.

prompt: Section 04's `add` refuses a negative session. What did `private(set)` add to that rule?
hint: What could a caller still do without it?

choices.text: It checks the sign of each number
choices.why: The `guard` checks; `private(set)` checks no values.

choices.text: Speed, since the array is no longer copied when it is read by `plan`
choices.why: Access levels do not change how values are copied.

choices.text: No caller appends around `add` any more
choices.why: Right: without it, `plan` could append `-30` directly and the `guard` would never see it.

choices.text: It makes `minutes` a constant
choices.why: The value still changes, through `add`.

prompt: `public class Reminder` in a library. What can another module NOT do with it?

choices.text: Create one with its public `init`
choices.why: Creating is using, and `public` allows using.

choices.text: Call its public methods
choices.why: Calling is using.

choices.text: Subclass it and override its methods
choices.why: Right: subclassing outside the module needs `open`.

choices.text: Store it in an array of `Reminder`
choices.why: Storing it is using it too.

prompt: A class is `open` and its method `text()` is `public`. Another module subclasses it and overrides `text()`. What happens?

choices.text: It compiles: an open class opens all its methods
choices.why: Each method is opened on its own.

choices.text: The subclass compiles and the override is refused
choices.why: Right: `overriding non-open instance method outside of its defining module`.

choices.text: The subclass is refused, and so is the override
choices.why: The class is open, so subclassing it is allowed.

choices.text: It compiles, and the library's `text()` runs instead
choices.why: Swift does not silently ignore an override; it refuses it.

prompt: Which of these can be marked `open`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A class
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A method of a class
choices.why: Yes: overriding is opened per method.

choices.text: A struct
choices.why: A struct has no subclasses, so `public` is its widest level.

choices.text: A protocol
choices.why: Protocols are adopted, not subclassed.

prompt: Where is a `package func` visible?

choices.text: Only in its own file
choices.why: That is `fileprivate`.

choices.text: In every module that imports its module, wherever it is
choices.why: That is `public`; `report` was refused.

choices.text: In every module of the same package
choices.why: Right: `plan` used it and `report`, another package, could not.

choices.text: Only in its own module
choices.why: That is `internal`, and `plan` is another module.

prompt: Before Swift 5.9, how did two modules of one package share a helper?
hint: Which level reached across a module boundary before `package` existed?

choices.text: With `internal`, the default
choices.why: Internal stops at the module.

choices.text: By making it `public`
choices.why: Right: every user of the library then saw it too, with a comment asking them not to call it.

choices.text: By copying the file into both targets
choices.why: That makes two different helpers in two modules, not one shared.

choices.text: Through `fileprivate` and a shared directory
choices.why: Fileprivate stops at the file.

prompt: `report` was refused because the boundary of the `package` level is the ___, the directory with one `Package.swift`.
hint: Not the module, and not the file.

prompt: Why is `Goals` an enum with no cases, rather than a struct?

choices.text: No `Goals` value is ever created by mistake
choices.why: Right: `'Goals' cannot be constructed because it has no accessible initializers`.

choices.text: Static properties work in enums only
choices.why: Structs and classes have them too.

choices.text: Enums are faster
choices.why: Nothing about speed: there are no instances at all.

choices.text: A struct would make `Goals.weekly` public
choices.why: Access is written per member either way.

prompt: `plan` declares its own `struct Week` and imports `PlannerCore`, which has one too. What does a plain `Week` mean inside `plan`?

choices.text: The library's, because it was imported first
choices.why: Order of imports does not decide it; the current module's name wins.

choices.text: Neither: the compiler refuses it as ambiguous
choices.why: The program built and ran.

choices.text: `plan`'s own, and the other is `PlannerCore.Week`
choices.why: Right: a name declared in the current module wins, and the module name reaches past it.

choices.text: Whichever of the two has an `init` that fits the call
choices.why: Name lookup chooses the type before any initialiser is considered.

prompt: In section 07, `Goals.weekly` is 300 and the week holds 200 and 150 minutes. What does `print(Goals.weekly - theirs.total)` print?
Match each need of the planner to the access level that meets it most narrowly.
hint: Narrowest that works, as section 02 advised.

pairs.left: A note log only `Week` and its extensions touch
A debug summary for `plan`, a module of the same package
A reminder class other packages may subclass

prompt: Order these from the narrowest region to the widest.
A library's `public func save(_ week: Week)` takes a `Week` that is `internal`. What does the compiler do?
hint: Could a caller outside the module name the parameter's type?

choices.text: It makes `Week` public to match
choices.why: The compiler never widens a level for you.

choices.text: It accepts it, and callers outside pass any value
choices.why: They could not even write the type of the argument.

choices.text: It accepts it and treats the function as internal
choices.why: It does not quietly demote a declaration; section 06 says it refuses it.

choices.text: It refuses the declaration
choices.why: Right: nothing can be used from further away than the things it mentions.
